candidates.finding: Durham's travel market is nearly balanced: 202,000 trips come INTO Durham from outside on an average weekday and 205,153 go OUT — an inbound/outbound ratio of 0.98. Roughly 2.1% of the region's 19.5M trips cross Durham's boundary in either direction.
caveats: Trip balance is not an economic-attraction measure; it counts trips, not jobs or shoppers.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Boundary exchange dial / two-arrow balance graphic opening 'Who Comes to Durham?'.

candidates.finding: The Durham day is a twin-peak day with the afternoon ahead: 156,056 trips start in the 08:00 hour and 161,115 in the 15:00 hour — the afternoon peak is the biggest of the day. The region is nearly still at 04:00 (5,674 trips) and survey-hours 24:00–27:00 hold just 8,072.
caveats: Departure time, not arrival time; 2022 full basis (ages 5+, all walk trips). Survey hours run 04:00–27:59.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Clock + volume curve synchronized with map animation (A Day in Durham).

candidates.finding: Boundary travel is a two-way river at every municipality: net imbalances are tiny relative to the exchange — Oshawa balances to 0.3% of its two-way flow and even Scugog, the most lopsided, sits at 3.2%. Gross exchange varies six-fold, from 15,423 (Brock) to 97,123 (Pickering).
caveats: Inbound counts all trips ending in the municipality from outside Durham (any household); outbound counts trips starting there to outside Durham.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Diverging net bars under gross-exchange columns — the flatness of 'net' IS the story.

candidates.finding: GO rail for Durham households is a downtown shuttle with a two-anchor front door: 8,644 of 18,736 GO trips (46.1%) touch Union as an alighting point, and Union is also the top boarding station (8,367) — the return legs. On the line itself, Oshawa GO Station (2,729) and Whitby GO Station (2,712) are nearly tied. Riders reach these stations overwhelmingly by car: 90.8% at Oshawa, though Pickering walkers reach 26.4% without one.
caveats: Station OD cells rest on few survey records (Union↔Whitby ≈146 records for 2,573 expanded trips) — rankings are safe, individual small cells are not. go_on/go_off identify GO rail stations; non-rail access geography uses trip origin/destination as proxy.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Lakeshore-East line diagram with station weights + access-mode strips (HOW DURHAM GETS TO GO).

candidates.finding: Each hour belongs to a different Durham. The 05:00 hour is 84.8% home-based work; by 08:00 school (36%) and discretionary dominate the peak; from 08:00 discretionary travel never gives the lead back. Even in mid-career hours the biggest single purpose by volume is discretionary, not work.
caveats: Broad purpose categories; shares of each hour's trip-starts.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Stacked purpose ribbon flowing through the day.

candidates.finding: 116,586 inbound trips (57.7%) end at Home — Durham residents coming back. The remaining 85,398 trips arrive for an activity in Durham: Usual Work, Shopping, Other Work-related lead, with "Usual Work" at 29.5% — meaning 70.5% of inbound activity travel is not commuting at all.

caveats: Detailed destination purpose of the Durham-ending leg, all surveyed households. 'Ends at Home' trips cannot be split resident vs visitor without a household filter, so they are treated as a separate class rather than assumed.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Two-tier donut: Home-ending vs activity inbound; ranked purpose bars inside (WHY PEOPLE COME).

candidates.finding: Durham's net exchange with the rest of the region swings hard across the day: net OUTFLOW bottoms at 07:00 (−15,134 trips in the hour) as residents leave, then flips to net INFLOW peaking at 17:00 (+10,474) as the day's trips come home. Durham is an origin at some hours and a destination at others.
caveats: Trips with a Durham endpoint and known start time; midnight+ survey hours excluded from the headline search. A trip's 'return' is its own departure, so net inflow hours are dominated by journeys home.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Net-flow line crossing zero over the day, paired with inbound/outbound bands.

candidates.finding: Coming to Durham and leaving it are near mirror images: driving carries 78.3% of inbound vs 77.6% of outbound boundary trips, and transit splits 6.9% vs 7.0%. The boundary effect is what vanishes: only 67 inbound trips are on foot, against 118,858 walking trips inside Durham — the boundary is crossed almost entirely by motor vehicles (92% counting passengers).
caveats: Boundary-crossing trips only, all surveyed households; small modes (cycle, motorcycle) have thin survey support at the boundary.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Back-to-back mode bars (inbound vs outbound) plus a 'what vanishes at the boundary' inset.

candidates.finding: Each mode lives at a different scale: the median reported trip distance is <1 km for walking, 1–2 km for cycling, 5–10 km for driving and 10–20 km for transit. 15.9% of drive trips are under 2 km straight-line — a pattern, not a verdict that they could have been walked.
caveats: Straight-line (not routed) distance; bands use reported whole km. Short auto trips are not automatically replaceable by walking or cycling.
candidates.possibleVisualization: One map that physically rescales per mode (EVERY MODE HAS ITS OWN MAP).

candidates.finding: Car dependence is climbed, then partly descended: children 5–14 drive nothing (they ride in 52.7% of trips and walk 24.7%); driving climbs through ages 15–24 (38.4%) to a peak of 84.9% at 45–64, then steps down after 65 (77.3% at 65–74, 72.9% at 75+) while being a passenger climbs back up to 20.8%.
caveats: Shares of each age group's trips; group sizes differ — never compare raw trip counts across ages without population denominators. Age is the trip-maker's age, household vehicles the context.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Age slope charts: drive/passenger/walk shares across six age bands (DURHAM CHANGES WITH AGE).

candidates.finding: The journey to the journey is often multi-link: among drive-access GO riders, 49.6% of GO journeys use 2+ transit links, vs 52.1% for drive-access local-transit journeys. n_route counts transit links, not public-facing transfers.
caveats: Two links generally imply a change between links, but n_route is a route-count, not a transfer count in the intuitive public sense.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Journey stack diagram: access → links → egress (THE TRANSIT JOURNEY).

candidates.finding: Purpose creates different geographies: 96.7% of home-based school travel stays in Durham vs 72.2% of home-based work; work sends 17.4% of its trips to Toronto vs school's 2.3%.
caveats: Durham-origin trips by Durham households; broad purpose only.
candidates.possibleVisualization: Purpose switcher on the network map (THERE ISN'T ONE DURHAM NETWORK).

candidates.finding: Each station has its own front door: car access (driven + dropped off) ranges from 90.8% at Oshawa down to 73.3% at Pickering, where 26.4% of riders simply walk to the platform. Catchments differ station by station.

candidates.finding: In zero-vehicle households transit+walk carry 61.9% of trips; in 3+-vehicle households they carry 5.8%. Association, not causation.
caveats: Household vehicle availability is associated with travel behaviour; this cross-tab does not prove causation. Households, not persons, are the vehicle unit.
